sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: An Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB) is any exogenous object that penetrates the ocular tunics and resides within the globe. It represents a subset of open-globe injuries (OGI) and requires urgent ophthalmic intervention. The severity is determined by the mechanism of injury, size, composition, and location of the object, as well as the presence of associated endophthalmitis or retinal detachment.

sections.title: The Siderosis Bulbi Cascade
content: 1. Iron IOFB undergoes oxidation in ocular fluids.
2. Ferrous ions (Fe2+) release and diffuse through tissues.
3. Free radical production via Fenton reaction leads to lipid peroxidation.
4. Selective damage to RPE, photoreceptors, and ganglion cells.
5. Progressive ERG changes (Initial supernormal A-wave, then b-wave depression).
6. End-stage Ocular Siderosis: Glaucoma, retinal pigmentary degeneration, and blindness.

sections.title: Pathognomonic Signs of Siderosis
content: Iris Heterochromia (affected eye becomes darker/rust-colored)
Fixed, dilated pupil (mydriasis due to iris sphincter damage)
Rusty anterior subcapsular lens opacities (Siderotic Cataract)
Pigmentary retinopathy (mimics Retinitis Pigmentosa)
Secondary Glaucoma (Iron deposition in Trabecular Meshwork)

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging Protocol
content: Step 1: Non-contrast Thin-Cut CT (1mm) of the Orbit - Gold Standard.
Step 2: X-Ray Orbits (Caldwell and Lateral views) - If CT is unavailable.
Step 3: B-Scan Ultrasonography - ONLY if globe is closed or intraoperatively; detects RD/VH.
Step 4: MRI - STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED unless metallic IOFB is 100% ruled out.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapidly worsening pain or hypopyon (Endophthalmitis)
Projecting metallic object (Do NOT remove in clinic)
Extruding intraocular contents (Uveal tissue/Vitreous)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (Optic nerve damage or massive RD)
Low Intraocular Pressure (Seidel positive or occult rupture)

Immediate Medical Management
content: NPO (Nothing by Mouth) for surgery.
Place a Rigid Fox Shield (No pressure on globe).
Update Tetanus prophylaxis.
Systemic Antibiotics: IV Vancomycin (1g Q12H) + Ceftazidime (2g Q8H) OR Oral Moxifloxacin (400mg Daily).
Antiemetics to prevent Valsalva (Ondansetron).

sections.title: Intravitreal Antibiotic Dosing
content: Vancomycin: 1.0 mg in 0.1 mL (Gram-positive coverage)
Ceftazidime: 2.25 mg in 0.1 mL (Gram-negative coverage)
Amikacin: 0.4 mg in 0.1 mL (Alternative for Ceftazidime)
Amphotericin B: 0.005 mg in 0.1 mL (If fungal/organic suspected)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Resident
content: Always look for an 'Entry Wound' — a self-sealing corneal track can be easily missed.
A 'Hole in the Iris' + 'Focal Lens Opacity' = IOFB until proven otherwise.
Siderosis can occur years after a forgotten injury; always ask about a history of metal-working.
If the IOFB is organic (wood), the risk of fungal endophthalmitis (Aspergillus/Fusarium) is extremely high.
In cases of multiple IOFBs (e.g., blast injury), prioritize the largest or most reactive ones.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Evidence
sections.content: The National Eye Trauma System (NETS) and the United States Eye Injury Registry (USEIR) provide the largest datasets on IOFB. Key findings include: 1) Early vitrectomy (within 24 hours) significantly reduces endophthalmitis risk. 2) Zone I injuries have better visual outcomes than Zone III. 3) The presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is the strongest negative predictor of final visual acuity.
